 Which USB-C Cable Do You Actually Need?
 Last updated: August 2026 
 The connector that fits everything, and guarantees nothing about what is inside the cable. Photo: Tony Webster, CC BY 2.0 
 Somewhere in your house is a drawer with eight black cables in it. Same oval plug, both ends, no markings that mean anything. One of them charges your laptop at full speed. Two of them charge it slowly enough that you assume the battery is dying. One will not drive a monitor no matter what you click. And you cannot tell which is which by looking, so you grab whichever is on top and hope.
 That is not carelessness. It is the predictable result of a connector that fits everything and promises nothing. Before USB-C, the plug told you what you had: fat rectangle for the printer, trapezoid for the camera, micro for the phone. Crude feedback, but feedback. USB-C removed it, and nothing on the outside is obliged to replace it.
 We wrote about why USB-C fragmented into so many incompatible cables a couple of weeks ago. This is the follow-up question, which is the one that costs money: given that mess, what should you actually own?
 Quick answer: two cables. A cheap certified 240W charging cable, several of them, one per room. And one short 40Gbps data cable, kept somewhere you can find it. That covers almost every household, and one of each costs somewhere between $30 and $45 at the time of writing.
 How we picked: We do not hands-on test cables, so this guide is built on specifications, on what USB-IF certification actually verifies, and on manufacturers’ own published figures. Where a claim looked like received wisdom, we went to the source: the USB Type-C logo guidelines, Apple’s and Google’s box-contents pages, and published sustained-throughput measurements rather than headline link rates. Cables go on sale hard, so treat every price here as a starting point.
 Everything comes down to three numbers
 A USB-C cable can differ from another USB-C cable in exactly three ways that matter to you.
 Power. How many watts it can carry without melting or lying about itself.
 Data. How fast it moves files, from 480 megabits per second to 80 gigabits per second, a spread of roughly 166 times.
 Video. Whether it has the wiring to carry a display signal at all.
 These three are independent, which is the part that catches everyone. A cable can be superb at one and hopeless at the others, and price tracks none of them reliably. Apple’s own 240W charging cable, about as premium as cables get, moves data at USB 2.0 speed. So does Anker’s. That is not a defect. It is a correct design choice for a cable whose job is power.
 Every comparison below sits inside one of those three columns.
 Power, compared
 The default for any compliant USB-C to USB-C cable is 3 amps at up to 20 volts, which is 60 watts. That covers a lot: phones, tablets, handhelds, the Nintendo Switch 2 (whose official adapter tops out at exactly 60W), and the MacBook Air, which now ships with a 40W adapter.
 Above 3 amps, the rules change. To carry 5 amps, the cable must contain a small chip called an e-marker, which lives in the plug and answers for the cable when the charger asks what it can handle. The cable is not a negotiator so much as a witness: interrogated once, believed thereafter. A cable that cannot vouch for itself does not get trusted with more than 60 watts, so the two ends quietly settle for something safe and nobody tells you.
 Tier 
 Volts × amps 
 What it covers 
 60W (the default) 
 20V × 3A 
 Phones, tablets, Switch 2, Steam Deck (45W), MacBook Air 
 100W 
 20V × 5A 
 Most 14in laptops, 65W handhelds like the ROG Xbox Ally X, docks 
 140W 
 28V × 5A 
 16in MacBook Pro, mobile workstations 
 180W 
 36V × 5A

 240W 
 48V × 5A 
 The current ceiling of the standard 
 One wrinkle in that table matters at the checkout. The top three tiers run at higher voltages, and they need a cable built and marked for 240W. A 100W cable will not carry 140 watts, however well made it is.
 240 watts is where USB Power Delivery stops. It was set in 2021 and has not moved since, which is unusually good news: buy at the top of the scale once and you are done.
 Who genuinely needs more than 60W? Fewer people than fear it. The 16in MacBook Pro ships with a 140W adapter and wants every watt, and the 14in asks for 96W to fast charge. The ThinkPad class of laptop, and handhelds like the ROG Xbox Ally X, sit just over the line at 65W, which is 20 volts at 3.25 amps and technically wants the 5-amp cable too, though they charge only a whisker slower on 60. Mobile workstations and gaming laptops draw more still, though most use a barrel plug and fall back to 100W over USB-C anyway.
 Phones, almost never. Apple publishes no wired wattage for the iPhone 17, only a promise of 50 per cent in 20 minutes from a 40W adapter; ChargerLAB put a meter on the 17 Pro Max and measured a peak of about 36 watts, with the standard 17 drawing less. The Pixel 11, launched this very week, is rated at 30W, and the Pro XL at 45W. Samsung’s Galaxy S26 Ultra advertises 60W, and Android Authority’s bench test found it holds that for about two minutes before settling near 48W. The 100W-plus figures on Chinese flagships have mostly required the maker’s own charger and cable, so a standard cable will not deliver them whatever its rating, though Xiaomi’s latest can finally hit full speed on standard Power Delivery. Charging is stranger than a wattage number suggests, which is the ground we covered on wireless charging .
 The comparison winner is not close. Buy 240W. It costs a couple of dollars more than a 60W cable, works with everything you own, and will still be correct in five years.
 Data, compared, and this is where the money goes wrong
 Now the fact that pays for reading this article.
 Most USB-C cables you own carry data at USB 2.0 speed. That includes expensive ones, and it includes nearly every cable that came in a box with a device. 
 This is not a guess. Apple’s own support page states it plainly: the USB-C cable that comes with your iPhone supports charging and USB 2 speeds, and USB 3 speeds require a different cable. Google is more direct still. Its Pixel box-contents page has listed the same string for a decade: “1 m USB-C to USB-C cable (USB 2.0)”. Samsung’s own 100W retail cable, a premium 5A accessory, publishes its data rate as 480Mbps.
 For charging, all of that is fine. Power does not travel on the data wires. For moving files it is the difference between a lunch break and a shrug.
 Speed tier 
 Real sustained throughput 
 25GB video file takes 
 USB 2.0 (480Mbps) 
 ~25 MB/s 
 about 17 minutes 
 USB 5Gbps 
 ~430 MB/s 
 about 1 minute 
 USB 10Gbps 
 ~950 MB/s 
 about 25 seconds 
 USB 20Gbps 
 ~1.8 GB/s 
 about 14 seconds 
 USB 40Gbps (USB4) 
 ~3.3 GB/s 
 about 8 seconds 
 USB 80Gbps (USB4 v2) 
 ~5.3 GB/s 
 about 5 seconds 
 Those are sustained rates from published drive tests, not headline link speeds, and they assume a drive fast enough to keep up. The conclusion is blunt: seventeen minutes against one minute is the gap between the cable in your drawer and a cheap 5Gbps cable. Everything above 10Gbps is refinement. Getting off USB 2.0 is the whole win.
 The trap on product pages. Wattage and speed are certified separately and marked separately. A cable can be branded 240W and still be USB 2.0 inside. The USB-IF publishes power-only logos for exactly that case, showing 60W or 240W and no speed at all, which is honest of them and completely lost on most shoppers.
 The comparison winner: one 40Gbps cable. Not because you need 40Gbps, but because the price gap between 10Gbps and 40Gbps has narrowed to a few dollars and 40Gbps is the tier that also guarantees you video and a docking station. Buy one, keep it short, use it deliberately.
 Video, compared
 Driving a monitor over USB-C uses DisplayPort Alternate Mode, which hands some of the cable’s high-speed wiring over to a display signal.
 Ports are allowed to skip it. Plenty of phones and cheaper laptops do, and nothing printed next to the socket says so. (USB4 and Thunderbolt machines are required to support it, one of the few guarantees in this whole business.) Cables are simpler and stricter: a USB 2.0 charging cable physically lacks the wires a display signal needs, and no setting will conjure them. The monitor sits there being black, with no error message, because nothing in the chain is designed to explain itself.
 If you use an external monitor over USB-C, your one good data cable is also your video cable. A certified 40Gbps cable has every wire connected, so it carries display signal by definition, which is the main reason to skip the 10Gbps tier and go straight to 40. If you have never plugged a monitor into a USB-C port, this section costs you nothing.
 Thunderbolt, and whether it matters to you
 Probably not. Let us be direct about it.
 Thunderbolt 4 and 5 are USB4 underneath, at 40Gbps and 80Gbps, with the optional parts made mandatory and a stricter certification programme behind them. Apple’s Thunderbolt 5 Pro cable is $69 for one metre at the time of writing. Third-party 80Gbps cables from Plugable and OWC run about $35.
 Who benefits: people running an external SSD as working storage, people with a dock driving two monitors, people pulling video off a card every week. If that is you, you already suspected as much.
 Everyone else is buying headroom they will never touch. A certified USB4 40Gbps cable does the same job for around $25 and will not bottleneck anything a normal household owns. Thunderbolt is a real technology solving a real problem, and it is not your problem.
 Reading the label without being fooled
 You do not need the history of USB naming. You need to survive a product page. Three things do that.
 The certified logo carries two numbers. A speed and a wattage: 40Gbps/240W, or 5Gbps/60W. Both numbers, on one mark, with the word CERTIFIED. That mark means the cable was submitted to the USB-IF compliance programme and passed the test suite for exactly those claims.
 There is no 10Gbps cable logo. This surprises people who go looking for it. The current cable logo guidelines define combined marks at 5, 20, 40 and 80Gbps only, because a 10Gbps and a 20Gbps cable are electrically the same cable. If a listing shows a 10Gbps cable logo, something is wrong with the listing.
 A power-only logo means USB 2.0 data. If the mark shows 240W or 60W and no speed, the cable is 480Mbps inside. That is the single most useful piece of label-reading in this whole business.
 Two honest caveats. Certification covers the sample the manufacturer submitted, not the unit in your box, and the USB-IF’s own product search warns that products certified more than two years ago “may fail the current iteration” of the programme. And the mark says nothing about how long the cable survives being yanked out of a laptop bag. It verifies claims, not durability. The USB-IF’s public product list is free to search if you want to confirm a specific model.
 Length, which nobody thinks about
 High speed over copper falls apart with distance. This is physics, not a manufacturing shortcut, and it is why buying long by default quietly costs you performance.
 Speed 
 Practical passive length 
 USB 2.0 (480Mbps) 
 up to 4m 
 5Gbps 
 up to 2m 
 10 and 20Gbps

 40Gbps (USB4) 
 0.8 to 1m 
 80Gbps 
 0.8 to 1m passive, longer requires active 
 Worth knowing: the lengths printed in the USB-C specification are reference values, not rules. What actually gets tested is signal loss, and a cable is compliant if the electrics pass, whatever its length. But those tests are why the lengths cluster where they do.
 Two consequences. A 3m cable is almost certainly a slow cable, which is fine if it lives behind the sofa charging a phone. And a 3m cable that genuinely runs at 40Gbps contains active electronics and is a different object at a different price. Apple’s 3m Thunderbolt 4 Pro cable is $159 at the time of writing, and when ChargerLAB cut one open they found an ARM processor inside each plug, retiming the signal before it fades. At that point you are not buying string. You are buying a small computer shaped like string.
 Rule of thumb: buy your charging cables long and your data cable short.
 What to actually buy
 Two cables. That is the entire recommendation.
 The charging cable, and buy several
 The workhorse: cheap, certified, one per room. Photo: Deergirl, CC0 
 Specification: USB-IF certified, marked 240W, any length that suits the room, USB 2.0 data and no apology needed for that.
 This is the workhorse. One by the bed, one at the desk, one in the bag, one in the car. At 240W it will charge anything you own including a 16in MacBook Pro, and being certified it will not do anything stupid while it does. Data speed is irrelevant here, so do not pay for it.
 Cables that meet the specification: Cable Matters’ USB-IF certified 240W cable has been selling in the $6 to $9 range at 2m, which is remarkable for a certified cable. Anker’s 240W cable is around $20 for a single, less in a multipack, and states that it meets the USB-IF specification. Apple’s own 240W cable is $29 for 2m if you want the woven jacket. Prices in USD at the time of writing.

 The data cable, and one is enough
 The one you fetch on purpose. Illustrative photo: Unsplash 
 Specification: USB-IF certified, 40Gbps, a metre or shorter, and check the wattage marking separately.
 This is the one you fetch on purpose when you are moving a card off a camera or plugging into a monitor. Keep it short, because 40Gbps and long do not coexist cheaply, and keep it somewhere you will find it in the dark.
 Watch the wattage on this tier, because it is where listings get confusing. Belkin’s USB4 cable is 40Gbps at 0.8m for around $25, but rated 100W rather than 240W. Belkin also sells a 240W cable at 20Gbps, a different product with very similar words on the box. Cable Matters does a certified 240W 40Gbps cable at around $24 for 1m. Wanting both numbers at maximum on one label usually means paying for Thunderbolt. For most people the 100W version is fine, since this cable’s job is data.

 The three situations that need a third cable
 You run a dock or two monitors. Buy Thunderbolt, 80Gbps, and stop reading buying guides about cables.
 You need a long run at speed. A 3m active cable, price checked before you fall in love with it.
 Your device charges on a proprietary protocol. Some phones hit their headline wattage only on the charger and cable they shipped with. Keep that cable, label it, and do not expect a standard cable to match it.
 That is the complete list. If you are not in it, two cables is genuinely the whole answer.
 And then label them
 The least glamorous advice here and the one that will actually change your week. Coloured tape, a paper tag, a marker on the plastic collar. Red for the fast one, nothing for the rest. Twenty minutes, once.
 It also stops you packing the wrong cable for a trip, which matters more than it sounds when you are already working out what you can take on a plane and running your battery through our power bank flight checker .
 How to test what you already own
 Before you buy anything, find out what is in the drawer. Your computer already reports the negotiated link speed of whatever is plugged into it, and that speed is the slowest link in the chain. Use a fast drive in a fast port, and if the number comes back low, the cable is the culprit.
 You need one fast external SSD (NVMe based, not a SATA drive in an enclosure, which caps around 500 MB/s and reads like a 5Gbps link no matter what).
 On a Mac. Apple menu, then System Settings, then General, then About, then System Report. Click USB in the sidebar. Each connected device shows a Speed line reading something like “Up to 480 Mb/s” or “Up to 10 Gb/s”. If your drive is not in the USB list at all, look under Thunderbolt/USB4, which means it negotiated a USB4 link and is good news rather than a fault.
 On Windows. There is no clean built-in readout for USB 3.x link speed, which is worth saying plainly because people hunt for it. Device Manager shows the hierarchy but no number. The nearest thing is for USB4 hardware: Settings, then Bluetooth and devices, then USB, then USB4 Hubs and Devices, which lists connected USB4 kit and its capabilities. For everything else, the free USB Device Tree Viewer by Uwe Sieber reads SuperSpeed link rates directly and needs no installation, though its 10 and 20Gbps readouts want Windows 11 24H2 or later.
 The universal version. Copy one large single file, 10GB or more, from a fast internal drive to a fast external SSD, and time it with your phone. Six or seven minutes means USB 2.0. Under half a minute means 5Gbps. Ten seconds means 10Gbps. Use one big file rather than a folder of small ones, or you are measuring filesystem overhead instead.
 Then vary one thing. Same drive, same port, different cable. If the number jumps, you have found the slow cable. Label it as a charging cable and move on.
 Frequently asked questions
 My laptop charges slowly. Is it the cable or the battery? 
Try a different cable before you conclude anything. A 140W charger paired with a 60W cable gives you 60 watts, silently. The most Windows will offer is a vague slow-charging notice, and even that never names the cable. If several cables behave identically, then it is worth checking your battery health or looking at the port.
 Is a more expensive cable a faster cable? 
No, and this is the central trap. Apple’s $29 240W cable is USB 2.0 for data. A $24 Cable Matters cable does 40Gbps. Price tracks build quality, brand and power rating, not speed.
 Do I need certified cables, or is that just a tax? 
The premium has essentially collapsed. Certified 240W cables now sell for single-digit dollars, so there is little reason to gamble. Out-of-spec USB-C cables have destroyed hardware in the past, one famously killing a Google engineer’s laptop during testing, which is why Amazon banned non-compliant ones from its marketplace in 2016.
 Can I use my old USB-A to USB-C cable? 
For charging a phone, yes, slowly. USB-A cannot do Power Delivery and cannot do video at all. If you are still charging from USB-A ports, replace the charger, not the cable.
 Is 240W overkill if I only have a phone? 
It is unused capacity, not a risk. A cable’s rating is a ceiling, not a dose, and devices draw what they need. The difference against a 60W cable is a dollar or two, so buy the higher number and stop thinking about it.
 The bottom line
 The connector removed the one signal people ever had, and the industry filled the gap with logos most shoppers have never learned to read. That is not a personal failing. It is a design decision you have been paying for.
 Buy a handful of certified 240W charging cables and one short 40Gbps data cable. Check the ones already in the drawer with a big file and a stopwatch. Label the good ones. Bin nothing, because a slow cable is still a perfectly good charging cable, and you have plenty of things that need charging.
 Then close the drawer, because you are done with this problem.
